prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- French parachutist Michel Fournier vowed Tuesday to try again to launch a record-breaking skydive in August, hours after a "freak" accident over Canada aborted his second attempt to do so. Michel Fournier tests his equipment a few days before his attempt to break four world records. "I'm not about to give up," the 64-year-old adventurer said of his shot at setting a world record for the highest jump and fastest, longest free fall by a man riding a balloon. Tuesday's attempt was thwarted when an electrical charge broke the cable connecting the balloon to the gondola, causing it to slip away from his ground crew and rise into the Saskatchewan skies over North Battleford. "The question is, why was it electrically activated?" said Michel Chevalet, a balloon expert working on Fournier's technical team. He suggested that static electricity may have been to blame but that it had been an unforeseen possibility. "Unexpected freak accidents do happen," he said.  Watch report on Michel Fournier's failed free-fall quest » . Fournier said the failure came as a blow. "It was like having a hammer over the head," he said.  Watch Fournier talk about trying again » . The former paratrooper had hoped his "Big Jump" would start 40 kilometers (25 miles) above the Earth's surface. But his hopes dissipated over the Canadian prairie shortly after 5 a.m. (7 a.m. ET), when the balloon took off before his capsule could be attached. Still clad in his bright yellow pressure suit, a visibly frustrated Fournier waved away cameras after his balloon's abrupt departure. It drifted back to the ground about 40 km away. Fournier says he spent nearly 12.7 million euros ($20 million) on his quest, a risky endeavor that French authorities refused to allow him to attempt over France. Canadian authorities approved the mission over the town of North Battleford, in sparsely populated Saskatchewan. The town's mayor, Julian Sadlowski, said Monday's failure was "a disappointment." "I thought this was going to be the day that we saw history made in the Battlefords," he said. Balloon trouble also doomed Fournier's effort to break the record in 2003. Fournier holds the French record for the highest parachute jump at 12,000 meters (40,000 feet). He says his next chance is in August because that is when the jet stream will next be favorable. The "Big Jump" will collect data that will help astronauts and others survive at high altitudes, he says. Fournier estimated that Tuesday's failed effort cost him and his sponsors about 600,000 euros ($946,000).

(CNN) — French skydiver Michel Fournier said Tuesday that he would make another attempt in August at a record-setting jump, only hours after an unusual accident in Canada brought his second bid to an end.

Several days before the planned leap, Fournier tested the equipment intended to help him break four world records.

“I’m not about to give up,” said the 64-year-old adventurer. His goal is to establish records for the highest parachute jump and the fastest and longest free fall by a man carried aloft by a balloon.

Tuesday’s mission failed after an electrical charge severed the cable linking the balloon to its gondola. The balloon escaped the ground crew and climbed into the sky above North Battleford, Saskatchewan.

Michel Chevalet, a balloon specialist on Fournier’s technical team, questioned what had triggered the electrical release. He said static electricity might have caused it, although the team had not anticipated that possibility.

“Unexpected freak accidents do happen,” Chevalet said.

CNN video reports showed Fournier’s unsuccessful free-fall mission and his comments about making another attempt.

Fournier said the setback was devastating, describing it as “like having a hammer over the head.”

The former paratrooper had planned for his “Big Jump” to begin 40 kilometers, or 25 miles, above Earth. Instead, shortly after 5 a.m. local time Tuesday—7 a.m. ET—the balloon lifted off over the Canadian prairie before his capsule had been connected.

Still wearing his vivid yellow pressure suit, Fournier appeared visibly upset and motioned for cameras to leave him alone after the balloon’s sudden departure. The balloon later returned to the ground roughly 40 kilometers away.

Fournier says he has invested almost 12.7 million euros, or $20 million, in the hazardous project. French officials would not permit him to carry it out over France, but Canadian authorities authorized the attempt near North Battleford, a town in the lightly populated province of Saskatchewan.

North Battleford Mayor Julian Sadlowski called Monday’s failure “a disappointment.”

“I thought this was going to be the day that we saw history made in the Battlefords,” he said.

A balloon problem also ended Fournier’s previous record attempt in 2003.

Fournier already holds France’s record for the highest parachute jump, having leaped from 12,000 meters, or 40,000 feet. He said August would be his next opportunity because the jet stream would not be favorable again until then.

According to Fournier, the “Big Jump” is also intended to gather information that could help astronauts and other people survive at extreme altitudes.

He estimated that Tuesday’s aborted attempt cost him and his sponsors approximately 600,000 euros, equivalent to $946,000.

**Balloon breaks free, halting French daredevil’s record skydive attempt**

**NORTH BATTLEFORD, Saskatchewan** — French adventurer Michel Fournier’s bid to make a record-breaking jump from the edge of space ended before liftoff Tuesday when his helium balloon broke free from its gondola and drifted away over the Canadian prairie.

Fournier, a retired French army officer, had planned to rise nearly 40 kilometers — about 130,000 feet — above Saskatchewan in a pressurized capsule before stepping into the stratosphere.

But during preparations near North Battleford, the massive balloon separated from the gondola while being inflated. Fournier was not inside the capsule, and no injuries were reported.

The mishap forced organizers to abort the long-planned mission, known as “Le Grand Saut,” or “The Big Jump.”

Fournier hoped the descent would break several records, including the highest parachute jump, the longest free fall and the fastest fall by a human. He expected to exceed the speed of sound before deploying his parachute.

The attempt was intended to surpass the benchmark set in 1960 by U.S. Air Force Capt. Joseph Kittinger, who jumped from roughly 102,800 feet.

It was the latest setback for Fournier, whose previous efforts had been delayed by technical problems and unfavorable weather. Organizers did not immediately say when—or whether—another attempt would be made.

## Static Charge Blamed for Michel Fournier’s Runaway Balloon

**NORTH BATTLEFORD, Saskatchewan —** French adventurer Michel Fournier’s attempt to make a record-breaking jump from the edge of space ended before he left the ground when an electrical charge apparently triggered the premature release of his giant helium balloon.

Fournier had planned to rise in a pressurized capsule to an altitude of roughly 40 kilometers—about 25 miles—over Saskatchewan and then leap back to Earth. The flight, known as **Le Grand Saut**, or “The Big Jump,” was intended to challenge records for the highest parachute jump, the longest free fall and the fastest human free fall.

During preparations, however, the balloon suddenly separated from the capsule and drifted away without Fournier. His team later said static electricity or another unintended electrical charge had activated the mechanism designed to release the balloon from the gondola. Once detached, the enormous, delicate balloon could not be recovered for another launch.

The accident destroyed one of the most expensive and technically demanding parts of the mission. Contemporary reports valued the lost balloon and failed launch at approximately **C$500,000**, although estimates varied. The broader Le Grand Saut project had cost millions of dollars over years of development, with Fournier selling personal property and relying on private sponsors to continue financing it.

Despite the setback, Fournier said he had no intention of abandoning the effort. He planned to obtain a replacement balloon, correct the electrical-release problem and return to Saskatchewan for another attempt in **August 2008**.

The mishap was the latest in a series of delays for Fournier, whose earlier plans had been disrupted by technical, financial and weather-related problems. He maintained that the project could contribute valuable information about high-altitude escape systems and human survival in the thin atmosphere near the edge of space.
